messages.subject: Multiplicative measurement error
parts:
Dear all,
 
I am trying to apply the SPDE model to fit some spatial data (x,y;h). Usually we assume h has multiplicative measurement error to some degree, saying 10%, i.e. h = h0+h0*e, where h0 is the true underlying spatial process and the measure error ratio e is around 10%. If I want to model the true spatial process h0 with the SPDE approach, what can I do with R-INLA? A simple approach I can come up with is to take log transformation, log(h) = log(h0)+log(1+e). In this way I can use the ordinary Gaussian family with assumptions on log(1+e) as additive error. But I am worried about two issues here: (1) my h lies in the real number range so that sometimes log(h) is not well defined; (2) I need to assume log(h0) to be the Gaussian process here, but I want h0 to be the Gaussian process. Could anyone help me with this problem? Thanks!
 
Kind regards,
Michael

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Multiplicative measurement error
parts:
Hi Michael,

On possibility is to linearise the model and iterate the inla estimations;
eta = x + x*e
would turn into
eta = -x0*e0 + (1+e0)*x + x0*e
where x0 and e0 are the posterior medians for x and e from the previous iteration.
This turns the problem into a sequence of problems that can be implemented in R-INLA.

We're working on methods for similar problems in a current project, but it's not ready to share yet.

Finn L

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Multiplicative measurement error
parts:
The needed parameter is weights= rather than scale=, but the real issue is inla only allows you to do that for already known weights (the predictor must be linear in all the latent variables). So the iteration/linearisation idea is based on the idea of using an estimate x0 of x as weight instead of x itself. The new estimate x is then the x0 needed for the next iteration.  The full linearisation I indicated can perhaps be replaced by only using weights=x0 in the formula you wrote, and ignore the rest of the full linearisation equation, but I can't guarantee the stability of that without doing maths...  But if it converges it's at least an easier solution.

There may be some other tricks for achieving the same thing.

Finn
